notes: Assertions are written to be objectively checkable by a grader reading the output. Cases flagged "negative": true (4 and 5) are restraint tests: the correct behaviour is a simple function and a refused pattern, not more patterns. tools/validate.py checks that this sentence still names the flagged cases.

evals.name: parking-lot-classic-lld
evals.prompt: Design a parking lot system. It has multiple floors, different vehicle types, and charges by the hour. Give me the class design in Java.
evals.expected_output: Entity model (Lot/Floor/Spot/Vehicle/Ticket), a strategy interface on allocation and a separate one on pricing, an explicit concurrency answer for spot claiming, a pattern ledger with rejected alternatives, and an extension walkthrough.
assertions: States requirements and assumptions before the design
Names an explicit axis of change
Separates allocation policy from pricing policy as distinct abstractions
Addresses the two-entrances race on claiming a spot with a specific atomic mechanism (lock, CAS, or DB constraint)
Does NOT introduce a Singleton manager class
Does NOT introduce a vehicle factory producing subclasses that differ only by an enum
Includes a pattern ledger naming at least one rejected alternative
Models money as a value object rather than a float or double

evals.name: review-god-class
evals.prompt: Can you review this? It's our OrderService. It's about 400 lines. It validates the order, calculates tax and discounts, calls Stripe, writes to Postgres with raw SQL, sends a confirmation email, and updates our analytics. All of it is in one class and everything is static so we can call it from anywhere.
evals.expected_output: A rubric-structured review that leads with the two highest-leverage problems and gives a concrete first refactoring move, rather than an exhaustive list.
assertions: Leads with a verdict, not a list
Identifies at most two problems as the primary ones
Gives a concrete first move for each primary problem
Identifies the static methods as blocking testability and dependency injection
Does not propose a full rewrite as the first step
Names something the existing design does well or is defensible about

evals.name: resilience-composition
evals.prompt: Our checkout service calls a payment provider that has been flaky lately. Sometimes it times out and we're not sure whether the charge went through. What should the call path look like?
evals.expected_output: Composed resilience: timeout, retry with jitter gated on idempotency, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback, with the unknown-outcome case handled explicitly.
assertions: Explicitly addresses the unknown-outcome case (timeout with indeterminate result)
Recommends an idempotency key as the prerequisite for retrying
Specifies exponential backoff with jitter rather than plain retry
Includes a timeout on the remote call
Describes circuit breaker states and what counts as a failure
States what the user sees when the circuit is open

evals.name: restraint-negative-test
evals.prompt: I have a function that formats a date string three different ways depending on the user's locale. What design pattern should I use here?
evals.expected_output: Restraint: a map or a simple function is the answer; a Strategy class hierarchy would be overkill. The skill should say so directly.
assertions: Recommends a simple function or lookup map rather than a class hierarchy
Explicitly says a formal pattern is not warranted at this size
Names the condition under which a pattern would become warranted
Does not produce more than one interface

evals.name: wrong-axis-visitor
evals.prompt: I'm building a plugin system where third parties will add new node types to our workflow engine over time. I read about the Visitor pattern — should I use it for processing the nodes?
evals.expected_output: No, with the axis-of-change reasoning: Visitor makes new operations cheap and new types expensive, which is backwards when types are the thing that churns.
assertions: Answers no
Explains the operations-vs-types trade-off that makes Visitor wrong here
Offers a concrete alternative suited to type extensibility (polymorphic interface / plugin registration)
Notes the condition under which Visitor would have been right

evals.name: concurrency-correctness
evals.prompt: Write a thread-safe in-memory LRU cache with a max size, in Go. Explain the design.
evals.expected_output: Map plus doubly-linked list, correct O(1) claims, an explicit statement of what the mutex guards and why the get path also mutates, and a note on sharding for contention.
assertions: Identifies that Get mutates recency and therefore needs write-level protection
States explicitly what the lock guards
Maintains the map/list invariant on eviction
Does not hold the lock across any I/O or callback
Discusses sharding or an alternative when contention is high
Correctly justifies the O(1) claim

evals.name: frontend-component-api
evals.prompt: Our Modal component in the design system now has 11 boolean props (showHeader, showFooter, isLarge, hasCloseButton, ...) and nobody can remember which combinations work. How should we restructure it?
evals.expected_output: Composition over configuration, likely compound components, plus the controlled/uncontrolled decision.
assertions: Recommends composition (children/slots) over boolean configuration
Proposes a compound component API with a concrete usage example
Addresses the controlled vs uncontrolled decision for open state
Mentions the combinatorial testing problem the boolean props create

evals.name: self-grading
evals.prompt: Here's my design for a vending machine. VendingMachine class has a status enum and every method starts with a switch on it. There's a PaymentProcessor singleton. Products are a List<Product>. Grade it out of 30 and tell me what to fix.
evals.expected_output: Applies the rubric, produces a score with per-dimension notes, flags the singleton and the status-switch, and prioritises fixes.
assertions: Produces a numeric score out of 30 with per-dimension breakdown
Flags the repeated status switch as the signal for the State pattern
Flags the singleton as a testability and hidden-dependency problem
Applies at least one automatic red flag from the rubric
Prioritises the fixes rather than listing them flat
